newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Gunmen strike again in north Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: Gunmen strike again in north Tanzania.

text.p: Gunmen posing as tourists shot dead a hotel cashier in northern Tanzania, three days after heavily-armed bandits ambushed 25 Italian and American tourists inside nearby Serengeti National Park.
Sources at the Impala hotel in Arusha confirmed Friday's report in Tanzania's Daily News about the murder of cashier Rose Mnango, 29.
They said she was killed on Wednesday when she pressed an alarm button, sensing three men were about to rob the foreign exchange bureau in the hotel, popular with tourists.
The men stole an unspecified amount of cash and escaped in a waiting car, the News said.
The killing confirmed a mounting security problem in and around Serengeti, one of Africa's best-known game parks.

Last Sunday about a dozen well-armed bandits ambushed four tourist mini-buses at a narrow bridge in the park. One bus escaped but two were shot up, seriously wounding two women tourists, one Italian and one American.
A third bus was also forced to stop and the bandits, using rifle-butts to club some victims, robbed the passengers of cash and valuables.
Tourism industry sources said the attack was one of the worst involving tourists in the park, but not the first, and security had to be improved.
Tour operators who organised the trip to Serengenti failed to publicly report the ambush, apparently fearing the impact on Tanzania's expanding wildlife tourism industry.

The head of the East African country's national parks (Tanapa), Lota Meramali, reported the attack on Tuesday in a statement at his headquarters in Arusha. The statement received little if any national publicity and reached Nairobi on Friday.
"Tanapa deeply regrets to report an isolated incident of armed robbery on tourist vehicles," it began. It said about 10 bandits were involved.
It said three victims had serious wounds: Italian tourist Anna Olvero, American tourist Mrs Becks and Tanzanian driver Godson Mtindi.
Tanapa said to boost security and find the bandits it had called park rangers back from leave, begun 24-hour patrols in Serengeti and deployed 12 patrol vehicles and an aircraft.
"The investigation is going on and a thorough search is continuing," Meramali told Reuters. He said 16 tourists were involved, perhaps discounting those on the bus that escaped.
Tourism sources in Arusha, at the foot of Mount Meru and the gateway to many of Tanzania's top attractions, said previous attacks had occurred at the same bridge.
"It is like a trap. You have to slow right down and the drivers can't get away if something happens," one source, who declined to be quoted by name, told Reuters.
